newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigerian fans on high for musician Fela's burial.
newsitem.headline: Nigerian fans on high for musician Fela's burial.

text.p: Marijuana smoke wafted through a crowd of several thousand fans gathered on Tuesday for the burial of Nigeria's Afrobeat music star Fela Anikulapo-Kuti, who died of AIDS.

There was barely space in the narrow streets around Fela's Lagos home for those who wanted to move to the beat of old hits played by the band of the singer, composer and saxophonist who popularised the continent's music across the globe.

"No president in the world could witness this kind of affection at his burial and it just goes to show what Fela means for this country," said student Bose Ladipo as Anikulapo-Kuti, known to his fans as Fela, was lowered into the ground near his home in a working class suburb of Lagos.
Fela, who became a star of the Nigerian and international music scene in the 1970s and 1980s, died of heart failure related to AIDS on August 2. He was 58.

Despite tears from some family members, sobriety was cast aside by most fans in a mood of celebration for Fela, who shunned convention and won a reputation for wearing only his underpants and openly smoking marijuana.

"I am going to do music until I die, man, Afrobeat music," said Seun Anikulapo-Kuti, Fela's 14-year-old son, who cried openly at the graveside. "Fela is not dead, he is still alive because his music lives on."
For many Nigerians, particularly youths and the poorest of the poor, Fela was a hero who challenged authority and stood against opression.

For successive military governments Fela was a dangerous irritant who sang songs insulting the intelligence of the soldiers who have ruled Nigeria for most of the years since independence from Britain in 1960.
He was detained on numerous occasions for a variety of offences and spent time in jail.

But over the past two years Fela made no public effort to challenge current military strongman General Sani Abacha, even though his younger brother, activist Beko Ransome-Kuti, is detained for alleged involvement in a coup plot.
Ransome-Kuti, 57, who is in solitary confinement at a northern prison was refused permission to attend the burial.
As the best-known Nigerian to die of AIDS, Fela has drawn attention to the spread of the HIV virus which causes the disease, in Africa's most populous nation of over 100 million people.
Doctors say millions of Nigerians are already infected with the virus and mistrust 1996 official figures which suggest less than four percent of the sexually-active population has the virus.

"Fela's death has helped to bring the existence and menace of AIDS in our society to the foreground, it has taken Fela's death for the nation to wake up," said the independent Guardian newspaper in its Tuesday editorial.
